newsitem.title: USA: ISDA disappointed by FASB derivatives decision.
newsitem.headline: ISDA disappointed by FASB derivatives decision.

text.p: The International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) said it was disappointed by the Financial Accounting Standards Board's (FASB) decision on derivatives accounting rules announced earlier on Thursday.
ISDA said it was unhappy that affected parties were not given an opportunity to determine impact of the new rules.

"Since FASB has made significant changes to what was proposed in its original draft, we believe that the final standard should be reviewed by a broad group, not just the Financial Instruments Task Force of FASB," ISDA Chairman Gay Evans said in a statement.
Earlier in the day, FASB said it had agreed to move ahead with a final statement on derivatives accounting standards, which included several changes from its 1996 proposals.

The rules basically require all derivatives to be recognized in financial statements and to be measured at fair value. Gains and losses would be accounted for depending on how a derivative is used and whether it is designated and qualifies for hedge accounting.
They key criterion for qualification is that the hedging relationship must be highly effective in achieving offsetting changes in fair values or cash flows.
FASB said the new standards would be simpler than the 1996 version because the effectiveness assessment would be based on the hedging entity's specified risk-management objective and strategy.

"This accounting standard will affect the ability of companies to manage risk," ISDA's Evans responded. "We are concerned that a 45-day, limited review of complex material which has changed significantly from the original exposure draft will not provide the Board with all the information it needs to make a final decision."
"It is more important to understand the impact of these changes than it is to meet an arbitrary deadline," she added.
"The derivative dealer and end-user communities should not be disenfranchised, and FASB should not deprive itself of the benefit of their views," she said.
FASB chairman Edmund Jenkins said earlier the new standard "addresses most of the concerns about our 1996 proposal expressed by constituents in comment letters and the public hearings."
